name: Bruin
tagline: A CLI-first data platform that bundles ingestion, SQL and Python transformations, orchestration, quality checks and lineage in one binary.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. The CLI is open source, so the paid surface is the hosted/cloud tier.

verdictSummary: The shape of Bruin is genuinely agent friendly: assets declared in YAML and SQL files, a DAG resolved from dependencies, quality checks as config, lineage derived from the queries. An agent can build a personal version of that loop in a weekend: a Python runner over DuckDB that topologically sorts asset files, renders Jinja, materializes tables, runs not-null and uniqueness checks, and emits a Mermaid lineage graph. What it cannot one-shot is the ingestion surface, which is hundreds of maintained source connectors, plus multi-warehouse dialect support and a hosted scheduler with alerting. Worth noting the Bruin CLI itself is open source and free, so a DIY build is really competing with the cloud tier, not the product. If your pipelines touch two systems and one warehouse, your own runner is fine; if they touch twelve, you are about to become a connector maintainer.
coreLoopDIY: A local CLI that reads YAML plus SQL asset files, resolves the dependency DAG, materializes each asset into DuckDB, runs declared quality checks, and renders a lineage diagram.
requirements: cron or a systemd timer for scheduling
credentials in .env if you pull from any real source
whatYouLose: Ingestion connectors: your build gets CSV, HTTP JSON and Postgres if you are lucky, not a maintained catalog of sources
Warehouse portability: a DuckDB-only runner does not speak BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift dialects
Hosted scheduling, retries, backfills and alerting that someone else keeps awake
Column-level lineage from real SQL parsing, as opposed to whatever you infer from dependency lists
Team surface: a UI, run history, permissions, and anyone but you understanding the pipeline
moatNotes: The connector layer is the expensive part, and it is expensive forever because upstream APIs keep moving.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the boring parts are the product. Writing a DAG runner is a pleasant weekend; keeping fifty source integrations working, handling incremental strategies and backfills correctly across four warehouse dialects, and having runs that fire at 03:00 without you is a job. People pay for the hosted tier to stop being the on-call engineer for their own orchestrator, and because pipeline definitions in someone else's format get stickier every quarter.
notes: The declarative core is very copyable; the connector catalog is not, which is exactly why the CLI can afford to be open source.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user data pipeline runner called "pipe" in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Python 3.11, uv for dependency management
- DuckDB as the only warehouse, file at ./warehouse.duckdb
- Typer for the CLI, Jinja2 for templating, PyYAML, rich for output
- No web server, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud anything

Pipeline format: a ./assets directory. Each asset is one .sql file with a YAML front matter block in a leading SQL comment containing: name, type (sql or python), depends (list of asset names), materialization (table or view), and checks (list like {column: id, check: unique} or {column: email, check: not_null} or {check: row_count_min, value: 1}). Python assets are .py files with the same front matter in a docstring, exposing a function materialize(con) that writes to DuckDB.

CLI commands:
- pipe validate: parse all assets, fail loudly on unknown dependencies, duplicate names, or cycles
- pipe run [--asset NAME] [--downstream] [--full-refresh]: topologically sort, render Jinja (expose ref('asset_name') to the resolved table name and vars from ./pipe.yml), execute, then run that asset's checks; stop the branch on failure but keep unrelated branches going
- pipe test: run checks only against existing tables
- pipe lineage [--out lineage.md]: emit a Mermaid graph of the DAG
- pipe seed: load every CSV in ./seeds into a table named after the file

Ingestion: implement exactly two loaders, chosen by a ./sources.yml file. One for HTTP JSON endpoints (paginated by page param, appends to a raw table) and one for Postgres tables via a DSN read from .env. Nothing else. Do not attempt a generic connector framework.

Runtime behavior: log each asset with duration and row count, write a JSON run record to ./.pipe/runs/, exit non-zero if any check fails so cron and CI can see it.

Explicitly out of scope: a UI, a scheduler (document a cron line instead), multi-warehouse dialects, incremental merge strategies beyond full refresh, column-level lineage parsing, and users or permissions.

Deliverables: working code, a sample pipeline with 3 assets and at least 2 checks that runs end to end from a seeded CSV, .env.example, and a README with the cron example and the asset front matter spec.
